title: Vaishali Rameshbabu Will Challenge for the World Chess Crown — And India Cannot Look Away
excerpt: The lowest-rated player in the Candidates field stunned the chess world in Cyprus. Now the 24-year-old from Chennai faces Ju Wenjun's four-time fortress in the most anticipated women's championship match in years.
body:
Vaishali Rameshbabu has done something no one predicted. The 24-year-old from Chennai, entering the Women's Candidates Tournament in Cyprus as the lowest-rated player in the field, emerged as its champion — and will now challenge China's Ju Wenjun for the Women's World Chess Championship in a match that could mark the most significant moment for Indian chess since her brother Praggnanandhaa's rise to the global elite.

## The Candidates: From Outsider to Champion

The eight-player double round-robin tournament, held at St. George's Hotel & Resort in Limassol from March 28 to April 16, was supposed to be a coronation for higher-rated favourites. Bibisara Assaubayeva and Zhu Jiner were considered the frontrunners; Vaishali was, by the numbers, the field's underdog.

She finished with 8.5 points out of 14 — a score built on relentless precision and an uncanny ability to convert half-chances. The decisive moment came in the final round, when she defeated Kateryna Lagno of Russia after a critical blunder by the experienced Grandmaster handed Vaishali a winning endgame. It was clinical, composed, and entirely characteristic of her playing style.

The victory earned her €65,400 in prize money and, far more valuably, a seat opposite Ju Wenjun in the title match.

## The Opponent: Ju Wenjun's Fortress

Ju Wenjun has held the Women's World Championship since 2018, successfully defending it four times. The Chinese Grandmaster is renowned for her deep preparation, psychological resilience, and the sheer difficulty of beating her over a 12-game match format.

Former champion Judit Polgár — widely considered the strongest female player in chess history — has publicly expressed doubts about Vaishali's chances, noting that Ju's experience in match play and her consistently high level of preparation create a formidable barrier. "Winning a candidates is one thing," Polgár observed. "A world championship match is an entirely different beast."

The dates and venue for the championship match remain undetermined by FIDE, but the 12-game format favours the more experienced player — at least on paper.

## A Family Affair

Vaishali's rise cannot be separated from the extraordinary story of the Rameshbabu family. Her younger brother, R. Praggnanandhaa, is already one of the top players in the open section and a household name in Indian chess. The siblings trained together in Chennai under the guidance of their father, who reportedly sold family assets to fund their chess education.

Their story has particular resonance for the Indian diaspora. Chess academies run by Indian-origin coaches have proliferated across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and the Gulf — and the Rameshbabu siblings are their most visible inspiration. When Praggnanandhaa reached the final of the 2023 World Cup, it was diaspora chess parents who celebrated loudest.

Now, with both a Rameshbabu and Gukesh Dommaraju — India's reigning Men's World Champion — in line for title matches in 2026, Indian chess stands at a historic zenith.

## What It Means for Indian Chess

India has produced female chess talent before — Koneru Humpy reached the world championship match, and Dronavalli Harika has been a consistent top-ten presence. But Vaishali represents something different: a generational shift, a player who came through the same hyper-competitive Indian chess ecosystem that has produced a generation of male superstars, and who now stands on the threshold of the sport's ultimate prize.

For the millions of Indian-origin children currently enrolled in chess programmes worldwide, from Fremont to Dubai, the message is unmistakable: the board does not discriminate. The only question is whether Vaishali's extraordinary run can survive the fortress that Ju Wenjun has built around the crown.


The championship match, when it comes, will be the most-watched women's chess event in history. India will make sure of that.
